As a reminder council enacted the triple bottom line policy in January of 2020 and it's important because it functions to embed sustainability into civic decision making triple bottom line enables us to consider and improve projects and programs.
And we're looking at how it supports the needs and well-being of both present and future generations by upholding environmental integrity equitable social systems.
Adjust economy and good governance.

So so far we have applied we're working on applying TBL to about 50 initiatives since the tools were developed and strong support from our leadership team and council have really helped with adoption.
Now that the TBL policy has been in place for over a year we've taken some time to reflect on lessons learned.
The tools being very useful for facilitating conversations between different subject matter experts, which can be uncomfortable at times.

We found the assessments conducted on projects that were nearly complete, found less opportunity to make improvements than those that are just beginning or at the stage of developing options.
So going forward we are trying to support project teams early on in development.
The the leap project was a two year multi city multi sector initiative led by the Canadian urban sustainability practitioners network with funding from the Federation of Canadian municipalities.

The leap project supported participating cities to including Saskatoon in the design and delivery of equitable clean energy programs that respond to the needs of low and moderate income households as well as other community members who have been underrepresented in existing clean energy programs.
Saskatoon was a leap of participants starting in early 2019 and it wrapped up in March of 2021.
The first phase involved creating an equity mapping tool to understand the impacts of energy poverty and household energy burdens in Saskatoon and other communities.
If you haven't checked out the tool it's online and I encourage you it provides some interesting layers on demographic information and understanding energy poverty in the city.
Each participating city then took a slightly different direction with.
With the project in Saskatoon the sustainability department led the delivery of the next phase which is the equity toolkit.

So the equity toolkit was created to play an equity lens to the sustainability departments work because we found our processes sometimes create more barriers to connecting with residents than we realize.
We wanted to address these barriers through all phases from inception to implementation.

We learned that equity deserving does not always mean low income, it can refer to communities that experience historical, social and environmental barriers based on age, ethnicity, disability, economic status, gender, nationality and many others.
The toolkit was developed as a how to guide based on best practice research and strengthen with feedback from community engagement.
It can be found on the city's website.
In creating the toolkit we realized that it would be beneficial to the entire corporation.
So integrating it into the TBL including more training videos and more support and communication is a next step we are pursuing.
And would help to increase the success of the equity and opportunity indicator of triple bottom line.
The toolkit how to guide is a 28 page document that includes key principles which are the best practices and ideals that we're striving for.

I think adding questions to consider throughout a project or program as it develops a checklist for success which sounds simple but it's a very thorough list of examples and practices for project managers to go through and incorporate into their projects.
The real world examples definitions and references.
We also created a one page summary document because we understand that a 28 page document can be overwhelming at first and it was a recommendation from our stakeholder engagement.
Of course this is a learning journey for us and when the equity toolkit went to the environment utilities and corporate services committee in June.

We see feedback that the section on colonialism wasn't clear and didn't reflect the message that we wanted to communicate and that colonial structures continue to create barriers and that we need to recognize these barriers to correct the systemic problems.
So we've updated it and we expect to continue to review and update the toolkit as we learn and learn more.
The toolkit was in draft phase with engagement ongoing. It was used to apply an equity lens to the design of the home energy loan program.
The water conservation strategy was also used as a case study to discuss the equity tool care was stakeholders.
So a few of the specific equity considerations incorporated into the design of the home energy loan program include.
The admin fee of $500 is way for income qualified participants and at first the stats Canada low income cutoff was used as the income threshold to be eligible.
However upon review and best practice to encourage equity this was increased to low income plus 50%.
No credit checks are required. The same low interest rate is offered to all residents regardless of their income or credit history interest rates are only dependent on the length of the term.
So 510 or 20 year terms the minimum loan is $1,000 which allows for small energy upgrades and the maximum loan of up to 60,000 is not dependent on the value of the home.
We've also tried to streamline the application process and communications because it is limited to single family home owners.
The health program does not address all equity concerns related to improving energy efficiency in our homes.
